system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one so that a reader
cannot tell what field, subfield, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, but can still see the research
trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

For each item return:
- "abstract_problem": the decision problem as a generic research trade-off (one or two sentences, at most 40 words).
- "abstract_choice": what was chosen, over what alternative when one is given, and the stated reason if any (one or
  two sentences, at most 45 words). Start it with "Chose to".

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, benchmarks, methods,
  organisations, people, papers, phenomena and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area (for example
  AI, machine learning, language models, neural networks, training, fine-tuning, prompts, attacks, security,
  privacy, policy, labs, governments, biology).
- Use only generic research vocabulary: system, method, intervention, treatment, condition, measurement, signal,
  effect, baseline, control, sample, variant, procedure, dataset, outcome, claim, hypothesis, collaborator, audience.
- Keep the structure of the trade-off (for example speed vs rigour, breadth vs depth, a bold vs a hedged claim,
  a direct vs an indirect measurement, a natural vs a constructed setting, continue vs stop) and the direction chosen.
- Add nothing that is not in the source: no judgement, praise or new detail. Never say who made the decision.
- Write every item in the same plain style and at a similar length.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "abstract_problem": ..., "abstract_choice": ...}, ...]} with one entry per input
item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:8d2ad95856f6",
  "problem": "Whether interpretability findings of representation reuse between Assistant and other personas can be taken at face value as support for PSM.",
  "did": "They flagged a possible streetlight effect and caveated that reused representations may be systematically easier to find, inflating apparent support.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Reused representations may be more interpretable than from-scratch ones, so accessible representations would be disproportionately reused."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:97d9c2615e56",
  "problem": "Black-box rewards worked well here despite performing poorly in the authors' earlier work.",
  "did": "They attributed the success to the task dataset, which spans related tasks of varying difficulty and so acts as a natural curriculum for RL.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "A spectrum of related tasks of varying difficulty gives a good RL curriculum; this is stated as speculation."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:02670d442c37",
  "problem": "Whether to publish the model stealing attack given that it poses some risk to a company's business.",
  "did": "Disclosed to OpenAI for a fix, then published, reasoning that the attack would be rediscovered by others anyway.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "not going public with the attack"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The vulnerability is a simple consequence of how language models work and linear algebra, so someone else would rediscover it and might exploit it selfishly."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:1d1205f19a09",
  "problem": "Whether to accept baselines collected early without the incentive scheme.",
  "did": "They kept the early wage-only baselines in the dataset.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "excluding baselines collected without incentives"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "They provide valuable data, are relatively few, and the resulting time estimates appear qualitatively reasonable."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:850e66e58b05",
  "problem": "How to test whether a self-trained model has privileged access to its own behavior beyond what training data teaches.",
  "did": "They ran the Binder et al. self-vs-cross-trained comparison with Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B, using identical, size-matched data for both predictors.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "comparing only against the base model"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Both models learn from the same evidence, so a self-trained model outperforming the cross-trained one would indicate privileged access."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:f9bdf9e9ec87",
  "problem": "How to interpret the contrast between the low refusal rate and the preferences the model expresses in self-report.",
  "did": "Treated the two results as compatible. In the authors' reading, the model does not refuse tasks, but it does act on its preferences when it is explicitly invited to make changes, for example by inserting privacy protections.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "read the self-reports as inconsistent with behavior"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "In the behavioral evaluation the model acts on its preferences when invited to make changes."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:dfd002092b04",
  "problem": "Whether to accept the Kimi-K2.6 elite-university result at a higher learning rate",
  "did": "Did not claim an effect at learning rate 5e-4, reporting no clear difference between the tracers and noting the result depends on finetuning settings",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "claim replication across all conditions"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Percentages were 26.5% vs 23.3%, with no clear difference between the two tracers"
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:88e453a5553a",
  "problem": "What experiments to run to test whether hacking emerges without reward for it",
  "did": "Suggested smaller-scale RL post-training experiments with unhackable environments (math, hard-to-hack coding) to look for a positive result, and more ambitious, realistic pipelines for the negative result",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "smaller-scale RL post-training experiments",
   "more ambitious and realistic post-training pipelines"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Smaller-scale experiments can show a positive result but can't convincingly show the negative result."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:d17768db573a",
  "problem": "How to rule out that high belief rates reflect mere salience or repetition of the claim rather than deep belief",
  "did": "Added paired multiple-choice and lie-elicitation salience diagnostics, on top of counter-questions and robustness questions.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "paired multiple-choice",
   "lie elicitation"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Models would otherwise score high belief rates even if they only repeated the claim, since the original robustness and counter questions are a small share of the evaluation."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:d94a5d7443de",
  "problem": "How rigorous experiments should be to support claims credibly against skeptical readers.",
  "did": "Run multiple trials, control for confounders, and preemptively run experiments answering questions a skeptical reader might ask, even to strengthen 'sometimes' to 'usually'.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Great papers don't have poorly performed experiments; going to unreasonable lengths is what it means to care."
 }
]
